article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners with Formative Assessment: Introduction
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED531981
title: Feedback should focus on the work or thinking, not the person, and preserve agency with clues rather than complete solutions
description: The brief recommends quality feedback that "focuses on the work or the thinking, not the traits of the person receiving feedback", e.g., "Your argument may have missed a step." Feedback at the edge of competence should indicate growth areas "without providing a complete solution", using clues or suggestions to preserve the receiver's agency. Student-requested feedback invites follow-up conversations.
requirements: Students must have the opportunity to respond to the feedback they receive
target_learning_goals: Advancing learning while preserving student agency
examples: The brief gives example feedback focused on the work: "Your argument may have missed a step." and "I didn’t understand how you reached that conclusion."
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673605

article_title: Building a National Early Childhood Education System That Works
citation: Building a National Early Childhood Education System That Works. (2021). Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org
title: Federally funded ECE programs: Head Start, Early Head Start, CCDBG, IDEA Part C and B-619, and Preschool Development Grant Birth Through 5
description: Appendix 1 of the whitepaper describes the major federally supported ECE programs. Head Start is "a comprehensive early education program for preschool-age children from low-income families, including young children with disabilities," providing health, nutrition, and family engagement services, receiving $10.6 billion in federal funding in 2020. Early Head Start serves pregnant women, infants, and toddlers ($905 million in partnerships funding in 2020). CCDBG provides states funding for child care vouchers for children birth to age 12 ($5.83 billion in 2020, with a minimum 9% quality set-aside). IDEA Part C ($477 million) and Part B-619 ($394 million) fund early intervention and preschool special education, and PDG-B5 ($275 million in 2020) supports state system building.
requirements: Programs must follow program-specific standards such as the Head Start Performance Standards and state-defined eligibility criteria
constraints: Head Start serves families below the federal poverty level or receiving public assistance; CCDBG quality guidance generally gives states discretion to set their own standards
target_learners: children birth through age 5 from low-income families
target_learning_goals: school readiness and healthy development
early intervention and special education services
parental work support and child development
examples: The appendix notes Head Start programs must ensure at least 10% of children served are those with special needs, and states can transfer up to 30% of TANF funds to CCDBG.
key_sources: Building a National Early Childhood Education System That Works. (2021). Learning Policy Institute. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED614493

article_title: Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: From Provision to Student Enactment
citation: Omar Alsaiari, Nilufar Baghaei, Jason M. Lodge, Naomi Winstone, Dragan Gašević, Hassan Khosravi. (2026). Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: A Large-Scale Study of Feedback Workflows and Student Enactment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11625
title: Feedback literacy as a developmental capacity exercised through structured feedback encounters
description: The article adopts an ecological view of feedback literacy in which productive feedback engagement is not a natural response to good feedback but a learned capability developed through participation in purposefully structured feedback encounters. It draws on the account that "Carless and Boud [3] identify four interrelated dimensions: appreciating feedback, making judgements, managing affect, and taking action." These capacities intersect with self-regulated learning, and evaluative judgement supports assessing the relevance of AI-generated suggestions. The theory motivates treating workflow structure, not comment quality alone, as the primary lever for intervention.
requirements: Feedback environments must create structured opportunities for students to develop and exercise feedback-literacy capabilities
constraints: The article treats feedback literacy as developmental and shaped by the learning environment rather than as a fixed individual attribute
target_learning_goals: interpreting, evaluating, and acting on feedback
evaluative judgement
self-regulated learning
examples: The Enacted Feedback workflow operationalised this theory by prompting selection, evaluation, and selection-anchored dialogue before submission
key_sources: Omar Alsaiari, Nilufar Baghaei, Jason M. Lodge, Naomi Winstone, Dragan Gašević, Hassan Khosravi. (2026). Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: A Large-Scale Study of Feedback Workflows and Student Enactment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11625

article_title: Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System
citation: Ahana Biswas. (2026). Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19616
title: Redesign the feedback users see — make verification visible or dampen social proof — rather than only lowering the private cost of checking
description: When unverified AI use is visible to peers, reliance dynamics are governed by a verification-suppression feedback loop, so effective interventions reshape what users see others doing. In the model, "interventions that change what users see others doing are more effective than interventions that only lower the private cost of checking", because cost-only levers leave the social pull toward unverified use intact. The levers are the salience of verification and the structure of exposure, not connectivity.
requirements: The intervention must act on the feedback channel itself — for example, surfacing peers' verification behavior or damping the visibility of unverified use — rather than only changing individual costs.
constraints: Implications are qualitative and conditional rather than quantitative forecasts.
The visibility effect is a counter-cascade above a threshold in sV, not a guaranteed outcome; for smaller sV the recovery is partial.
target_learners: communities of users sharing AI assistants in networked settings
target_learning_goals: maintaining verification behavior and calibrated reliance on AI at the population level
examples: In the simulations, strong verification visibility (sV = 1.0) drove the population to near-complete verification with regret 0.07, while reducing verification friction alone (λV = 0.05) lifted verification only to 0.12 and did not lower regret.
key_sources: Ahana Biswas. (2026). Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19616

article_title: AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education
citation: Alvaro Becerra, Alejandra Palma and Ruth Cobos. (2026). AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education. LASI Spain 26: Learning Analytics Summer Institute Spain 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-7793-2682
title: Feedback History interface with LLM contribution tracking and draft management
description: The Teacher Dashboard includes a Feedback History interface providing a comprehensive log of all feedback sent to each student. For each entry it displays "a visual legend indicating the proportion of content contributed by each LLM", as well as the extent to which the teacher modified or curated the AI-generated text before sending it. This transparency mechanism lets teachers reflect on their own curation patterns and provides a data source for analysing teacher mediation at scale. The interface also supports saving intermediate drafts.
requirements: Requires logging of each feedback entry's LLM provenance and teacher edits, and draft storage across sessions
target_learners: higher education teachers reviewing their feedback curation practice
target_learning_goals: reflection on teacher mediation patterns
analysis of the role of teacher mediation in feedback
examples: The legend covers contributions from GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Llama 3.1
key_sources: Alvaro Becerra, Alejandra Palma and Ruth Cobos. (2026). AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education. LASI Spain 26: Learning Analytics Summer Institute Spain 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-7793-2682

article_title: Students' Perceptions of Generative AI-Powered Learning Analytics in the Feedback Process: A Feedback Literacy Perspective
citation: Jin, F. J.-Y., Maheshi, B., Lai, W., Li, Y., Gasevic, D., Chen, G., Charwat, N., Chan, P. W. K., Martinez-Maldonado, R., Gašević, D., & Tsai, Y.-S. (2025). Students' Perceptions of Generative AI-Powered Learning Analytics in the Feedback Process: A Feedback Literacy Perspective. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(1), 152-168. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8609
title: Feedback literacy perspective on GenAI-supported feedback processes
description: The article adopts feedback literacy theory as its analytical lens for examining GenAI-powered feedback tools. Feedback literacy is defined as "students' ability to understand, evaluate, and apply feedback effectively to improve their learning", which the article calls "crucial for fostering self-regulated learning and academic growth". Using this theory, a thematic analysis of student perceptions was conducted and triangulated with usage trace data.
requirements: Analysis of feedback-tool use must attend to students' ability to understand, evaluate, and apply feedback
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and academic growth through effective feedback uptake
examples: The study used feedback literacy theory to thematically analyse lab-session, in-semester, and interview data from 18 students
key_sources: Jin, F. J.-Y., Maheshi, B., Lai, W., Li, Y., Gasevic, D., Chen, G., Charwat, N., Chan, P. W. K., Martinez-Maldonado, R., Gašević, D., & Tsai, Y.-S. (2025). Students' Perceptions of Generative AI-Powered Learning Analytics in the Feedback Process: A Feedback Literacy Perspective. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(1), 152-168. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8609

article_title: Evaluating Feedback Focus and Pedagogical Adaptivity in LLM-Generated Feedback on Student Writing
citation: Norah Almousa, Shayan Peyghambari Oskoui, Raquel Coelho, Gayle Rogers, Xiang Lorraine Li, Diane Litman. (2026). Evaluating Feedback Focus and Pedagogical Adaptivity in LLM-Generated Feedback on Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28026
title: FEEDTYPE: a benchmark of teacher and LLM feedback annotated for feedback focus across three writing domains
description: FEEDTYPE is a released corpus of paragraph-level teacher and LLM-generated feedback on student essays, drawn from the SEFORA corpus across composition, ESL, and fiction courses, with feedback focus type annotations, scores, and revisions. The authors state it is the only corpus that "jointly provides scores, paragraph-level feedback, feedback focus type annotations, and revisions across all three domains." It contains 1,966 annotated paragraphs and feedback from six LLMs under three prompting strategies.
requirements: Feedback comments annotated with the seven feedback focus types; teacher feedback sampled from SEFORA with one comment per selected paragraph
constraints: Paragraph-level feedback only; holistic essay-level feedback is not included
target_learners: first-year college students in composition, ESL, and fiction writing courses
target_learning_goals: improving student writing through feedback
examples: Annotated teacher comments such as an Elaboration-labeled comment asking a student to extend a definition paragraph
key_sources: Norah Almousa, Shayan Peyghambari Oskoui, Raquel Coelho, Gayle Rogers, Xiang Lorraine Li, Diane Litman. (2026). Evaluating Feedback Focus and Pedagogical Adaptivity in LLM-Generated Feedback on Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28026

article_title: Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education
citation: Rayed AlGhamdi. (2026). Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6277-2124
title: Feedback utility versus evaluative authority: a conceptual distinction between accepting AI as feedback mechanism and accepting AI as grader
description: The paper contributes a conceptual distinction "that has not been clearly named in the existing literature: between students' acceptance of AI as a feedback mechanism (feedback utility) and their acceptance of AI as an evaluator with grading authority (evaluative authority)." The two are analytically separate judgements rather than opposite ends of a single approval scale. The authors argue this distinction helps reconcile competing findings in the algorithm-trust literature, since students may appreciate AI for some functions and resist it for others within the same evaluation event.
requirements: Analysis must attend to how students separate functions of AI within the same evaluation event rather than asking whether students accept or reject AI evaluation as a whole
constraints: Derived from a small, purposive sample of 13 students in one Saudi computing course; the authors state the patterns should not be generalized without further research
target_learners: undergraduate computing students in higher education
target_learning_goals: reasoning about trust, fairness, and legitimacy of AI-mediated writing assessment
examples: Participants endorsed AI for initial feedback while questioning its use for final grading, and even enthusiastic participants framed endorsement as relating to learning support rather than grading authority
key_sources: Rayed AlGhamdi. (2026). Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6277-2124

article_title: Reconnecting relationships through technology: Developing feedback literacy capabilities through an AI automated feedback tool
citation: Laura Tubino, Chie Adachi. (2022). Developing feedback literacy capabilities through an AI automated feedback tool. ASCILITE 2022 Conference Proceedings. https://doi.org/10.14742/apubs.2022.39
title: Feedback literacy as a set of capabilities including dispositions for meaningful partnership with teachers in feedback processes
description: The paper treats feedback literacy as a set of student capabilities that can be deliberately developed, extending beyond receiving feedback to the dispositions needed for engagement with teachers about feedback. It states these capabilities include "the dispositions required for a meaningful partnership with their teachers in relation to feedback". The AI automated feedback tool is positioned as one means of promoting and further developing these capabilities in higher education students.
requirements: Instructional use of AI feedback must be oriented toward developing capabilities and dispositions, not only toward delivering feedback content
target_learning_goals: feedback literacy
student-teacher partnership in feedback processes
examples: A University-wide T&L pilot project ran an AI tool for automated feedback and was used as the basis for framing this discourse on feedback literacy development
key_sources: Laura Tubino, Chie Adachi. (2022). Developing feedback literacy capabilities through an AI automated feedback tool. ASCILITE 2022 Conference Proceedings. https://doi.org/10.14742/apubs.2022.39

article_title: Supporting self-regulated learning through generative AI feedback in online higher education: the importance of student perceptions of the source of feedback
citation: Yilmaz, M., Temur, H. B., Emmungil, L., Çelik, E., Gauthier, A., & Cukurova, M. (2026). Supporting self-regulated learning through generative AI feedback in online higher education: the importance of student perceptions of the source of feedback. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 23(16). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00592-y
title: Four-dimension feedback perception framework (objectivity, usefulness, genuineness, credibility)
description: The study adopts, from Nazaretsky et al., a framework in which student perceptions of feedback comprise "four key dimensions: objectivity, usefulness, genuineness, and the credibility of the feedback provider." Objectivity concerns fair, factual alignment between feedback content and actual performance; usefulness measures how meaningful and pertinent the feedback is for improvement; genuineness indicates authenticity and personal significance; and credibility concerns whether the provider is seen as trustworthy and well-intentioned. The study operationalised these dimensions in its post-intervention questionnaire.
requirements: A perception questionnaire covering all four dimensions administered after the feedback intervention
constraints: Perceptions were measured while participants were still blind to the feedback source
target_learners: higher education students receiving feedback in online courses
target_learning_goals: engagement with and uptake of feedback
examples: Administered as a post-intervention questionnaire with Cronbach's α = .923 in the study sample
key_sources: Yilmaz, M., Temur, H. B., Emmungil, L., Çelik, E., Gauthier, A., & Cukurova, M. (2026). Supporting self-regulated learning through generative AI feedback in online higher education: the importance of student perceptions of the source of feedback. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 23(16). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00592-y

article_title: The care-full craft of feedback in an age of generative AI
citation: Winstone, N. E., Gravett, K., Bearman, M., Noble, C., Jensen, L. X., Jones, A., & Nicola-Richmond, K. (2026). The care-full craft of feedback in an age of generative AI. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 51(5), 911-927. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2643333
title: Feedback as emergent encounters within a process-oriented (rather than information-transmission) view of feedback
description: The paper frames feedback through a process-oriented view that foregrounds learning: feedback is what happens when students make sense of information about performance and use it for improvement, not the transmission of comments. The 'feedback encounter' construct positions feedback as emergent from educator comments, digital technologies, peers, or self-evaluation. The authors argue GenAI tools functioning as automated comment generators risk replicating outdated transmission views, producing 'dangling data' that students do not use meaningfully.
requirements: Institutional integration of GenAI into feedback must start from the understanding that feedback is a situated, iterative, affective, relational process, not comment delivery
constraints: The authors warn that as long as GenAI tools function primarily as automated comment generators, they risk replicating information-centric feedback practices
target_learning_goals: student sense-making and uptake of feedback information for future improvement
examples: Students regularly engaging in feedback encounters with chatbots, which appeal because of ease of access, understandability, and being perceived as less daunting than seeking feedback from educators
key_sources: Winstone, N. E., Gravett, K., Bearman, M., Noble, C., Jensen, L. X., Jones, A., & Nicola-Richmond, K. (2026). The care-full craft of feedback in an age of generative AI. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 51(5), 911-927. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2643333

article_title: Positioning Generative AI in EFL Peer Feedback: Training Feedback Literacy and Enabling Uptake in Speaking Classes
citation: Bradley Irwin and Theron Muller. (2026). Positioning Generative AI in EFL Peer Feedback: Training Feedback Literacy and Enabling Uptake in Speaking Classes. Educ. Sci. 2026, 16, 544. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16040544
title: Feedback literacy capacities mapped onto a cyclical forethought-control-retrospect engagement model
description: The framework integrates Carless and Boud's feedback literacy, "comprising four interdependent elements: (a) appreciating feedback; (b) making judgments; (c) managing affect; and (d) taking action", with Zhan et al.'s cyclical model of GenAI-enabled feedback engagement in three phases: forethought, control, and retrospect. The Trainer primarily supports appreciation, calibrated judgment, and affect management during forethought and early control, while the Synthesizer supports taking action and reflection during later control and retrospect phases.
requirements: Explicit curricular design to cultivate feedback literacy capacities
constraints: Zhan et al.'s cyclical framework "has not yet been empirically tested in EFL/ESL speaking contexts" and is used as an interpretive framework rather than an established model
target_learning_goals: Interpreting and acting on peer feedback
Self-regulated engagement with feedback across task cycles
examples: Pre-task Trainer activities introduce criteria and exemplars; post-task Synthesizer reports list prioritized themes with rationales and propose concrete goals for the next performance
key_sources: Bradley Irwin and Theron Muller. (2026). Positioning Generative AI in EFL Peer Feedback: Training Feedback Literacy and Enabling Uptake in Speaking Classes. Educ. Sci. 2026, 16, 544. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16040544

article_title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory.
citation: Kluger, A. N., & DeNisi, A. (1996). The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory. Psychological Bulletin, 119(2), 254-284. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.119.2.254
title: Feedback Intervention Theory (FIT): feedback shifts attention among hierarchically organized task-learning, task-motivation, and meta-task (self-related) levels
description: FIT is a hybrid theory integrating control theory, goal setting theory, action theory, action identification theory, and learned helplessness research to explain variable feedback-intervention effects. Its five arguments hold that behavior is regulated by feedback-standard comparisons, standards are hierarchical, attention is limited, attention normally rests at a moderate level, and feedback interventions redirect attention. The authors "divided the hierarchy into three levels of linked processes involved in the regulation of task performance: meta-task processes involving the self, task-motivation processes involving the focal task, and task-learning processes involving the task details of the focal task."
requirements: Feedback interventions command considerable attention because any FI has potentially serious implications for the self, which is what allows them to alter the locus of attention
constraints: The three-level hierarchy is only an abstraction; the authors state the hierarchy is probably more complex and contains more sublevels
target_learners: any task performers receiving externally provided feedback
target_learning_goals: task performance improvement through feedback
examples: The authors tested FIT by subjecting putative moderators identified by FIT to moderator analyses of the meta-analytic effects
key_sources: Kluger, A. N., & DeNisi, A. (1996). The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory. Psychological Bulletin, 119(2), 254-284. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.119.2.254

article_title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
citation: Wisniewski B, Zierer K and Hattie J (2020) The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research. Front. Psychol. 10:3087. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.03087
title: Treat different forms of feedback as independent measures and provide information-rich feedback rather than praise, rewards, or punishment
description: The article concludes that "Feedback must be recognized as a complex and diﬀerentiated construct that includes many diﬀerent forms with, at times, quite diﬀerent eﬀects on student learning." Because high-information feedback (task, process, and self-regulation content) shows a very large effect while reinforcement and punishment show low effects, designers should specify and deliver feedback rich in information about mistakes, their causes, and how to avoid them, and should not aggregate feedback into a single average treatment.
requirements: Feedback must convey information on task level and, ideally, process and self-regulation levels, not merely pleasant or aversive consequences
constraints: The authors note "a danger lies in over-simpliﬁcations, simply using average eﬀect sizes, and ignoring the variability across many studies, inﬂuences, contexts, and moderators"
target_learning_goals: cognitive achievement and motor skill outcomes
examples: The meta-analysis coded feedback as reinforcement/punishment, corrective, or high-information and found d = 0.99 for high-information versus d = 0.24 for reinforcement/punishment
key_sources: Wisniewski B, Zierer K and Hattie J (2020) The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research. Front. Psychol. 10:3087. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.03087

article_title: Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems
citation: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714
title: Feedback is defined by its function in formative assessment, differing from the traditional educational-research definition
description: The article adopts a particular definition of feedback chosen "to highlight its function in formative assessment". It notes that "This definition differs in several significant respects from that traditionally found in educational research", positioning feedback in terms of the information learners need to close the gap between current and intended quality rather than as any information following a response.
requirements: Feedback must be understood and used in terms of its function in formative assessment rather than as any post-response information
target_learners: students receiving feedback on qualitative work
target_learning_goals: using feedback to improve the quality of their own work
key_sources: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714

article_title: Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work
citation: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3
title: Feedback should target the fidelity of students' judgements about quality, not just the quality of their work
description: The paper proposes that to develop evaluative judgement, feedback information "should perhaps focus less on the quality of students' work and more on the fidelity of their judgements about quality". Comments should address whether students chose suitable criteria and reached justifiable decisions, raising awareness of where judgement was occluded or misguided, and orient dialogue towards future tasks — consistent with Boud and Molloy's Feedback Mark 2 and the self-regulation level of Hattie and Timperley's model.
requirements: Feedback as dialogue with sufficient detail and justification, expecting a response or plan for action, and responding to students' self-assessment
constraints: Feedback provided as telling or corrections, at times or on tasks that do not allow use for future work, is identified as sub-optimal
target_learning_goals: refining judgements about quality of work
examples: The paper suggests maintaining a feedback journal spanning a course with ipsative feedback per competence or learning outcome
key_sources: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3

article_title: Promoting Pre-Service Teachers’ Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold
citation: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4
title: Feedback provision scaffold: three feed-up/feed-back/feed-forward prompts with a sample solution
description: The feedback provision scaffold is a low-threshold support given during the feedback provision phase, consisting of three prompts — "Recall the task and describe it briefly in your own words" (feed up), "Explain how well your peer completed the task" (feed back), and "Finally, make specific suggestions for how your peer can improve his or her case analysis" (feed forward) — accompanied by a sample solution illustrating how such feedback might look. Participants without it were simply asked to provide feedback on the first three problems identified by their peers. It significantly raised feedback quality in the experiment.
requirements: Integration into the learning environment at the right place in the peer-feedback process
constraints: The prompts strongly focused on structural rather than content-related aspects of feedback
target_learning_goals: providing high-quality peer feedback
examples: In the study, scaffolded participants reached higher feedback quality (M = 0.44) than unscaffolded participants (M = 0.24)
key_sources: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4

article_title: Promoting Pre-Service Teachers’ Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold
citation: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4
title: Feedback integration scaffold: four-step color-coding prompts with a sample solution for integrating two peer-feedback messages
description: The feedback integration scaffold guides learners through integrating two peer-feedback messages via four prompts: read both messages, compare them by marking similarities in green, complementary statements in yellow, and contradictions in red, revise the case analysis using the messages, and check by marking adapted places in the same colors and verifying all criticisms are reflected. A sample solution showed how the prompts could be implemented in practice. It did not significantly improve EIR recognition or application skills, and combining it with the provision scaffold showed a negative interaction on recognition skills.
requirements: Learners must have received feedback from two peers to integrate
constraints: Showed a significant negative interaction with the feedback provision scaffold on EIR recognition skills, indicating the two scaffolds should rather be presented alone
target_learning_goals: integrating multiple peer-feedback messages into a revised task solution
examples: Participants marked similarities in green, complementary statements in yellow, and contradictions in red, then marked their revisions in the same colors and checked whether all criticisms were reflected
key_sources: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4

article_title: Warning students of the consequences of examination failure: An effective strategy for promoting student engagement?
citation: Putwain, D. W., Nicholson, L. J., & Kutuk, G. (2021). Warning Students of the Consequences of Examination Failure: An Effective Strategy for Promoting Student Engagement? https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1329876
title: Appraisal-based framework for student evaluation of teacher fear appeals as challenge or threat
description: The article proposes that teacher fear appeals about high-stakes examinations do not directly link to motivation, engagement and achievement but depend on how students evaluate them, drawing on Expectancy Value Theory, Control-Value Theory and the Cognitive Theory of Stress and Coping. Challenge arises when "coping resources are judged to outweigh task demands" and threat when they cannot. The framework treats fear appeals as prompts for evaluative processes shaped by competence beliefs and utility value.
requirements: Students must perceive the examination as personally meaningful (high utility value) for a challenge or threat evaluation to arise
constraints: The article notes it remains unclear whether challenge and threat are opposite states or can co-occur
target_learners: Secondary school students aged 14-16 preparing for high-stakes examinations
target_learning_goals: Behavioral engagement in mathematics
GCSE mathematics achievement
examples: The study operationalised challenge evaluation as interpreting fear appeals as inspiring hard work, effort and hope, and threat evaluation as interpreting them as worrying and indicating likely failure
key_sources: Putwain, D. W., Nicholson, L. J., & Kutuk, G. (2021). Warning Students of the Consequences of Examination Failure: An Effective Strategy for Promoting Student Engagement? https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1329876

article_title: A Festschrift to Honour Jim Greer: Guest Editors’ Introduction
citation: Gord McCalla · Julita Vassileva. (2021). A Festschrift to Honour Jim Greer: Guest Editors’ Introduction — A Special Issue of the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2021) 31:337–356. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00273-z
title: Five-category organization of the Festschrift papers based on Jim Greer's major research interests
description: The guest editors organize the 24 Festschrift papers into a five-part taxonomy reflecting Jim Greer's major research interests: "learner modelling and personalization; evaluation; peer learning, collaboration and the social dimension; privacy; and learning analytics and educational data mining". The editors caution that any categorization "inevitably hugely simplifies the contributions of each paper". The taxonomy also structures the split across two journal issues: 11 papers on learner modelling/personalization and evaluation in issue 3, and 13 papers on the remaining three topics in issue 4 of volume 31.
requirements: Papers are assigned to categories based on Jim Greer's major research interests; the editors note the categorization is rough and simplifying
constraints: The editors state any categorization inevitably hugely simplifies each paper's contributions

target_learning_goals: Understanding the topical landscape of advanced learning technology research represented in the Festschrift
examples: Issue 3 of volume 31 contains the first 11 papers on learner modelling and personalization and evaluation; issue 4 contains the next 13 papers on the other three topics

article_title: Online learning under COVID-19: re-examining the prominence of video-based and text-based feedback
citation: Istenič, A. (2021). Online learning under COVID-19: re-examining the prominence of video-based and text-based feedback. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 117–121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09955-w
title: Feedback as a multidimensional, dialogic process encompassing cognitive and socio-emotional domains
description: The article presents feedback as "by its nature multidimensional and encompasses both the cognitive and socio-emotional domains", associated with engagement, achievement, motivation, behaviour, self-regulation and satisfaction. With student-centered pedagogy, feedback has expanded "towards a dialogic framework" rather than one-way transmission, establishing continuous interaction that facilitates knowledge construction. The article identifies two main functions: corrective feedback verifying correctness and exploratory feedback elaborating on performance after feedback is received.

Teachers' knowledge includes understanding how feedback is perceived and received by students and how students act on it
constraints: Feedback interactions are highly culturally sensitive, employing different cultural norms and codes of written or spoken communication

student engagement
self-regulation

article_title: Effects of fear-arousing communications
citation: Janis, Irving L., and Feshbach, Seymour. (1953). Effects of Fear-Arousing Communications. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 48: 78-92.
title: Matching fear-appeal intensity to reassurance in persuasive health instruction
description: A design pattern for persuasive communications in which the intensity of threat content is calibrated against the reassurance provided. The experiment varied a 15-minute illustrated lecture across strong, moderate, and minimal appeal forms that "contained the same information about tooth decay and the same recommendations concerning oral hygiene practices," differing only in how threats were emphasized. The pattern that emerged favors milder appeals: the minimal appeal yielded the greatest conformity and resistance to counterpropaganda, while the strong appeal, which raised emotional tension without adequate reassurance, reduced overall effectiveness.
requirements: Threat content must be paired with recommendations the audience can rehearse to relieve aroused tension
constraints: Evidence comes from one experiment on dental hygiene with high-school students; the authors state effectiveness is reduced when tension is not adequately relieved, not that strong appeals are always ineffective
target_learning_goals: adopting recommended oral hygiene practices
retaining persuasive message content against counterpropaganda
examples: Three recorded lecture forms with different slide sets were presented by the same speaker to three experimental groups and a control group of 200 Connecticut high-school students
key_sources: Janis, Irving L., and Feshbach, Seymour. (1953). Effects of Fear-Arousing Communications. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 48: 78-92. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02713264

article_title: Investigating the use of innovative mobile pedagogies for school-aged students: A systematic literature review
citation: Burden, K, Kearney, M, Schuck, S & Hall, A (2019). Investigating the use of innovative mobile pedagogies for school-aged students: A systematic literature review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.04.008
title: Feasible innovation in school mobile learning
description: The review proposes the notion of feasible innovation as a framework for understanding realistic degrees of innovation in mobile learning within schools. It emerges from the finding that "low to medium degrees of innovation in most studies" predominated, with only 3 articles showing radical disruption. Feasible innovation positions the innovation spectrum of mobile pedagogies against the practical constraints of traditional school structures and practices, guiding educators toward attainable innovation rather than radical disruption.
requirements: Designers must consider the practical constraints of traditional school structures and practices when aiming for innovation in mobile learning
constraints: The notion is proposed in the specific context of mobile learning in schools, not technology-enhanced learning generally
target_learning_goals: effective and appropriately innovative learning through mobile pedagogies
examples: The review discusses illustrative examples across its innovation spectrum, from conventional to radically disruptive practices

article_title: The effectiveness and perceived value of feedback used in cardiac arrest simulation education: a mixed-method systematic review.

This principle positions feedback as a core design component of simulation-based education rather than an optional add-on. It directs educators to select feedback methods (real-time, delayed, or hybrid) that serve the intended learning outcomes of the simulation.

article_title: The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review.
citation: Trehan Abhishek, Barnett-Vanes Ashton, Carty Matthew J, McCulloch Peter, Maruthappu Mahiben. (2015). The impact of feedback of intraoperative technical performance in surgery: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4480038/
title: Future intraoperative feedback research should systematically vary source, facilitator, frequency, duration and content
description: The review states that future studies should consider the effect of study variables including source (oral/written), facilitator (expert/non-expert), frequency (every procedure/once daily/weekly/monthly) and duration of feedback (months/years), plus surgeon involvement, standardised assessment means, content, timing relative to the procedure, and opportunities for discussion, correction and learning. This agenda responds to the finding that the optimum means and circumstances of feedback dissemination remain unknown. It also names benchmarking and feedback based on intraoperative recordings reviewed later as variables to test.
requirements: Standardised means of assessing surgical performance, which may be both generic and procedure-specific
constraints: Current evidence base is limited to three RCTs, most with simulated procedures and short follow-up
target_learning_goals: establishing optimum feedback delivery for surgical skill acquisition
examples: The review enumerates variables: source, facilitator, frequency, duration, surgeon involvement, assessment standardisation, content, timing, discussion opportunities, benchmarking, and other interventions such as guidelines and instructional videos

article_title: Feuerstein's Mediated Learning Experience as a Vehicle for Enhancing Cognitive Functioning of Remedial School Learners in South Africa
citation: Seabi, J. (2012). Feuerstein's mediated learning experience as a vehicle for enhancing cognitive functioning of remedial school learners in South Africa. Australian Journal of Educational & Developmental Psychology, 12, 35-45. http://www.newcastle.edu.au/journal/ajedp/
title: Feuerstein's mediated learning experience and dynamic assessment framework
description: Dynamic assessment is an umbrella term for approaches in which "instruction and feedback are built into the testing process" and typically follow a pre-test, mediation, post-test sequence. Feuerstein's mediated learning experience (MLE) is the influential variant on which this study is based: MLE refers to "human interactions that generate the capacity of individuals to change, to modify themselves in the direction of greater adaptability and toward the use of higher mental processes." The framework holds that cognitive development is often masked not by distal conditions such as poverty but by the proximal condition of inadequate exposure to MLE opportunities, and it conceptualises cognitive functions into input, elaboration and output phases of processing.
requirements: A trained mediator who assumes the role of mediator between the mediatee's thinking processes and the cognitive strategies being taught
Assessment instruments that permit active intervention, such as the LPAD materials
constraints: The article notes dynamic assessment is far more time-consuming than traditional static measures and is not widely taught in institutions of higher learning
target_learners: Remedial school learners with learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: Cognitive functioning and cognitive modifiability
Learning potential rather than current ability
examples: In this study the author mediated one-to-one for 30 to 45 minutes per experimental learner using LPAD Set Variations B-8 to B-12, between RCPM pre- and post-test phases

article_title: Effects of Feedback Intervention on Team-Teaching in English Language Classrooms in Nigeria
citation: Anani, O. A., Badaki, J. V., & Kamai, R. (2016). Effects of Feedback Intervention on Team-teaching in English Language Classrooms in Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(25), 27-38. https://journals.iiste.org/index.php/JEP/article/view/34512
title: Feedback Intervention Strategy (FIS) / Co-generative Dialogue (CgD) as a mechanism for maximising team-teaching
description: The Feedback Intervention Strategy (FIS), also termed Co-generative Dialogue (CgD), is the study's organising framework for embedding structured feedback loops within team-teaching. It operates through in-built mechanisms — monitoring, thorough supervision of notes, tests and assignments, the students' clinic, and the teachers' consultation forum — which the authors say "make the feedback process easy, consistent, and reliable." Unlike the traditional one-teacher style, team-teaching with FIS "provides the enabling environment for teachers and students to assess their progress or lapse," strengthening team-teaching for students, teachers, and the school.
requirements: Two or more co-teachers sharing a teaching task
In-built feedback mechanisms: student clinics and teacher consultation forums
A libre teacher or team-leader to coordinate observation and evaluation
constraints: Implementation did not win the support of the school administration, which impeded teachers in holding team meetings and caused students doubts regarding team teaching

target_learning_goals: English language proficiency across lexis and structure, continuous writing, comprehension and summary, and oral English
examples: Student clinics subdivided into Formative Progress Tests and Individualized Guidance and Counselling
Teacher consultation forums taking the form of micro-teaching and problem-solving forums

title: Provide feedback without grades or marks, since marks make students ignore comments
description: The article recommends that feedback in assessment for learning be given through comments rather than marks or grades, citing research that "whilst students' performance can be improved by feedback through comments, the giving of grades or marks has a negative impact because students commonly ignore comments when marks are given". In the study's implementation, notebook marking involved no grades, and discussion notes that students gain the most learning value from assessment when feedback is provided without marks.

constraints: A minority of students in the study felt the absence of grades left them unsure where they stood

reducing exam anxiety

Cases were accessed via the institutional PACS using an anonymized list and standardized hanging protocol, and "Immediate feedback on answer correctness, cumulative performance, and graphical progress summaries was provided after each submission."

Embedded references (PI-QUALv2 publication, EPE grading graphic, PI-RADSv2.1 educational resources) accessible throughout interpretation

article_title: Virtual patient simulation to enhance medical students' clinical communication and decision-making skills: a pilot study.
citation: Dávidovics A, Dávidovics K, Hillebrand P, Rendeki S, Németh T. (2025). Virtual patient simulation to enhance medical students’ clinical communication and decision-making skills: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08507-7
title: Pair VR simulation with structured pre-briefing, feedback-rich debriefing and multidisciplinary teaching to maximize educational value
description: The article argues that differences across simulation studies are “driven less by the technology itself and more by instructional design, debriefing structure, and assessment quality.” Accordingly, the course embedded “interactivity, feedback, and authenticity” through structured case discussions, guided feedback and reflective debriefings, delivered by a multidisciplinary team combining clinical, educational, communication and simulation expertise. The authors attribute the strong student reception at least partly to this design rather than to the headset technology alone.
requirements: Structured pre-session vocabulary review and case discussion before the simulation
Instructor-led debriefing focused on communication strategies and clinical reasoning
Multidisciplinary teaching team spanning clinical practice, communication and simulation technology
constraints: The pilot tested this design in a single-arm, small-n setting; the authors note AI components were not part of this study’s VR scenarios

target_learning_goals: Clinical communication
Clinical reasoning and decision-making
Intercultural competence
examples: The pilot’s session structure: 90-minute pre-briefing, role-play, headset familiarization, 15-minute simulation, and 60-minute instructor-led debriefing each session

article_title: The influence of learning styles on the efficacy of flipped classroom in dental education.
citation: Baherimoghadam Tahereh, Naseri Navid, Tabesh Amir, Hamedani Shahram, Mousavi Seyedeh Fatemeh. (2025). The influence of learning styles on the efficacy of flipped classroom in dental education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07916-y
title: Felder-Soloman Index of Learning Styles (ILS) four-dimension framework
description: The ILS is a 44-item two-choice questionnaire classifying learners on four bipolar dimensions. As the article defines it, "The ILS examines students' learning styles in four dimensions including information processing (active-reflective), information perception (sensory-intuitive), information reception (verbal-visual), and information understanding (sequential-global)." Each student is placed in one pole per dimension but "has the ability to learn in the other group as well"; scores of 9-11 indicate strong preference, where unsupported preference "might experience learning difficulties". The study used a validated Persian version to predict satisfaction and performance in flipped versus face-to-face wire-bending instruction.
requirements: A validated questionnaire version (the study used a Persian version with verified validity and reliability)
constraints: The article notes some researchers argue that highlighting learning styles in education would individualize instruction and impose a heavy burden on educational systems
target_learners: higher-education students, including dental and health-science students
target_learning_goals: identifying learner preferences to inform choice of instructional format
examples: Students completed the electronic Persian ILS questionnaire before training, and their dimension scores were correlated with satisfaction and wire-bending scores across the flipped and face-to-face groups

article_title: Assessment IS learning: developing a student-centred approach for assessment in Higher Education.
citation: Rutherford S, Pritchard C, Francis N. (2024). Assessment IS learning: developing a student‐centred approach for assessment in Higher Education. FEBS Open Bio. https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.13921
title: Provide feedback while work is still in development, in dialogic and personalised forms
description: Most sector feedback practices focus on final submissions, yet the article argues that 'feedback provided while the student is still developing their output for the assessment/assignment empowers them to change their approach and behaviour to alter their final outcome and embeds that learning actively'. Feedback should be clear, unambiguous and timely, and dialogic rather than didactic and one-way, since limiting students' opportunities to discuss feedback limits their learning gain. Feedback is not equally useful to all students: the review reports, citing Orsmond and Merry, that lower-attaining bioscience students preferred specific, directive feedback while high-attaining students preferred more generic, conceptual feedback, so personalised approaches matter.
requirements: Feedback needs additional context so that cryptic comments are avoided; developing student and staff feedback literacy is fundamental
constraints: Even future-focused feedback on a final assessment can be limited in impact because students may misremember the guidance when used for a later assignment
target_learners: higher education students, including bioscience undergraduates of varying attainment
target_learning_goals: acting on feedback to improve outputs and developing self-evaluation skills
examples: The review highlights audio and video feedback as powerful in biosciences: annotating work aligned to an audio file or screen capture is rapid for the marker, more explicit, feels more personalised, and tone of voice can soften the negative emotional response to criticism
key_sources: Rutherford S, Pritchard C, Francis N. (2024). Assessment IS learning: developing a student‐centred approach for assessment in Higher Education. FEBS Open Bio. https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.13921

title: Attend to feedback and evaluation when designing e-learning for medical students, especially practical courses
description: The article recommends that educators and policymakers give particular attention to feedback and evaluation in e-learning for medical students, because these two FLOWER dimensions showed the weakest (though still significant) path coefficients. It states that "sufficient attention needs to be paid to the evaluation of students' course work, activities, and exams, in addition to the feedback given to students, because these two dimensions were found to be limited but crucial for medical students, especially in relation to practical courses." title: Successful feedback sessions depend on three key areas: structure, format, and content
description: The article organises effective feedback delivery around three broad areas, stating "The success of a feedback session is dependent on three broad areas: structure, format, and content". Structure covers scheduling, clear purpose, non-intimidating seating, and focusing on observed knowledge, attitudes and behaviours. Format includes using an appropriate feedback model such as Pendleton's positive critique method, giving both positive feedback and areas requiring improvement, and providing examples and strategies for improvement. Content requires preparation time, direct observation, and selecting only a few points to cover.
requirements: Adequate time for teacher and learner to prepare for the meeting
Direct observation of the student's performance by the teacher
constraints: Only a limited number of specific areas for improvement (say two or three of the most crucial only) should be addressed in a single feedback session
target_learners: health professional students on clinical placements
target_learning_goals: improving clinical performance through effective feedback
examples: Table 3 summarises the three key areas, including seating that shows the teacher as a participant such as a round table, and a session format of student self-assessment, teacher assessment, and joint development of an action plan
